title: Diagnosis and Management of Mixed Transcortical Aphasia Due to Multiple Predisposing Factors, including Postpartum and Severe Inherited Thrombophilia, Affecting Multiple Cerebral Venous and Dural Sinus Thrombosis: Case Report and Literature Review
case_prompt:
A 38-year-old obese woman (BMI 30), on postpartum day 18 after a cesarean delivery at 30 weeks for severe preeclampsia, presented with a 2-day history of severe (8/10) headache and acute moderate right‐sided weakness. Several hours before presentation she developed difficulty speaking and understanding, although she was able to repeat words and sentences. She denied fever or trauma.  
On examination, temperature was 36.8 °C, blood pressure 150/100 mm Hg, heart rate 94 bpm. Ophthalmologic exam showed papilledema. Neurologic examination revealed an alert but agitated patient, right hemiparesis (MRC 4/5), right central facial paresis, and no meningeal signs. Language assessment demonstrated initial mutism followed by nonfluent speech with echolalia, absent spontaneous output, good articulation, preserved repetition, severe anomia, and markedly impaired auditory and reading comprehension (alexia and agraphia), consistent with mixed transcortical aphasia.  
Noncontrast head CT in the ED showed hyperdense straight sinus, vein of Galen, and left lateral mesencephalic vein; venous infarction of the left thalamus, basal ganglia, external and internal capsules, and corona radiata with hemorrhagic transformation in the head and corpus of the left caudate nucleus. MRI of the brain revealed left hydrocephalus, rightward ventricular compression, and slight hemorrhagic transformation in the left basal nuclei and thalamus. MR venography demonstrated near-complete occlusion of the superior sagittal sinus, straight sinus, vein of Galen, and the left deep venous system, with partial occlusion of the left transverse and sigmoid sinuses and left internal jugular vein.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Global aphasia was considered but “global aphasia can be ruled out (as in our case)…” because repetition was relatively preserved.  
2. Transcortical sensory aphasia was excluded since “depressed verbal fluency ratings indicate that transcortical sensory aphasia can be excluded (as in our patient)…”.  
3. Transcortical motor aphasia was excluded because “poor auditory comprehension performance excludes transcortical motor aphasia (as in our case)…”.  
4. A watershed cortical infarct causing mixed transcortical aphasia was considered but dismissed since “The most important cause of mixed transcortical aphasia is represented by cortical lesions isolating the intact perisylvian language areas… which was not the case here.”  
5. A subcortical lesion producing mixed transcortical aphasia fit the findings, as “Another etiology for mixed transcortical aphasias is due to subcortical lesions, including large thalamic hemorrhages… (as in our case)”.  
6. Cerebral venous thrombosis was suspected given imaging, because “The hyperdense appearance of the straight sinus, Galen vein, and lateral mesencephalic vein on the CT scan performed in ED was considered as a possible sign of cerebral venous thrombosis…”.
